title: ALERTCalifornia cameras flag a night fire near Auburn, and Cal Fire sends engines before anyone calls 911
summary: DigitalPath's smoke-detection software on ALERTCalifornia cameras flagged a fire near Auburn at 2:33 a.m. on 6 July 2024, before any 911 call, and crews kept it to a 30 x 30 foot area.
account: The University of California San Diego operates the ALERTCalifornia camera network, which runs AI smoke-detection software from DigitalPath of Chico, California. Cal Fire uses the network. At 2:33 a.m. on 6 July the network posted an alert of a fire near Auburn, in the foothills east of Sacramento. The report, from September 2025, gives the day but not the year. It places the case among the previous year's fires, so the record dates it to 2024. Nobody had called 911. Cal Fire's Grass Valley Emergency Command Center verified the alert and sent engines. Crews put the fire out before it spread beyond a 30 x 30 foot area. Cal Fire Deputy Chief Brian York said that in 2024 the cameras picked up 1,668 of the 7,553 fires in Cal Fire's jurisdiction. The cameras detected 636 of those fires before any person called 911. By October 2026 the network had grown to nearly 1,300 cameras. The program director planned 1,800.
purpose: The software detects smoke in camera feeds and alerts fire dispatchers automatically. The benefit in this case matches that purpose.
system: ALERTCalifornia camera network with DigitalPath AI smoke detection
developer: DigitalPath (AI smoke detection); ALERTCalifornia, University of California San Diego (camera network)
deployer: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (Cal Fire)

display.answer: Two syndicated articles by Rogers, republished by FireRescue1 and Phys.org, carry Cal Fire's account of the Auburn fire and Deputy Chief Brian York's figures. Reuters, KSBY and The New York Times report other fires and the network's growth. The governor's office issued its own press release in 2023.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: DigitalPath's smoke-detection software on ALERTCalifornia cameras flagged a fire near Auburn at 2:33 a.m. on 6 July 2024, before any 911 call, and crews kept it to a 30 x 30 foot area.
fields.account: The University of California San Diego operates the ALERTCalifornia camera network, which runs AI smoke-detection software from DigitalPath of Chico, California. Cal Fire uses the network. At 2:33 a.m. on 6 July the network posted an alert of a fire near Auburn, in the foothills east of Sacramento. The report, from September 2025, gives the day but not the year. It places the case among the previous year's fires, so the record dates it to 2024. Nobody had called 911. Cal Fire's Grass Valley Emergency Command Center verified the alert and sent engines. Crews put the fire out before it spread beyond a 30 x 30 foot area. Cal Fire Deputy Chief Brian York said that in 2024 the cameras picked up 1,668 of the 7,553 fires in Cal Fire's jurisdiction. The cameras detected 636 of those fires before any person called 911. By October 2026 the network had grown to nearly 1,300 cameras. The program director planned 1,800.

produced_by: A fixed camera network with 24/7 AI smoke detection covering remote terrain
A dispatch center that verifies AI alerts and sends crews without waiting for a 911 call
must_hold: A human verifies the alert before dispatch. The same source reports false positives from dust and clouds
Crews can reach the fire while it is still small

echoes.setting: Cleveland National Forest, about 50 miles east of San Diego, California; fire at 3 a.m. after the AI program began 10 July 2023; AI alerted a fire captain, about 60 firefighters responded, fire out within 45 minutes per Cal Fire (Reuters, 11 August 2023)
La Panza Ranch, San Luis Obispo County, California; ALERTCalifornia AI notified Cal Fire of smoke with no public 911 call; fire held to about 16 acres (KSBY; Paso Robles Daily News, 29 October 2024)
